sources.title: NIH ODS: Exercise and athletic performance
sources.summary: Reviews evidence, label interpretation and safety for protein, creatine, arginine, BCAA, caffeine and other exercise-supplement ingredients.
sources.limitations: A broad reference, not an independent test of products in this catalog.

sources.title: Morton et al.: Protein supplementation and resistance training
sources.summary: Across 49 trials involving 1,863 participants, protein supplements modestly improved training-related gains in strength and fat-free mass.
sources.limitations: Healthy adults undertaking resistance training; results do not establish that one commercial brand is superior.

sources.title: Kreider et al.: ISSN creatine position stand
sources.summary: Reviews evidence supporting creatine monohydrate for repeated high-intensity exercise and training adaptations.
sources.limitations: A narrative position statement, not a head-to-head trial of every form. Read the authors’ disclosed commercial relationships.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Ashwagandha for stress, anxiety and sleep
sources.summary: Small, short trials suggest possible improvements in stress and sleep, with substantial variation in extracts and study methods.
sources.limitations: Long-term safety and the best preparation remain uncertain. Liver, thyroid and medication concerns require attention.

sources.title: Chandrasekhar et al.: Ashwagandha root extract and stress
sources.summary: A 60-day placebo-controlled study enrolled 64 adults with chronic stress and reported improved stress measures with a specific root extract.
sources.limitations: Small and short; findings do not establish equivalence for root powders, other extracts, or blends.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Omega-3 fatty acids
sources.summary: Reviews EPA and DHA, dietary sources, cardiovascular research and safety. Outcomes depend on the preparation and clinical context.
sources.limitations: Prescription omega-3 treatments and ordinary retail fish oil are not interchangeable evidence.

sources.title: Manson et al.: Marine omega-3s in the VITAL trial
sources.summary: In 25,871 US adults, marine omega-3 supplementation did not significantly lower the primary major cardiovascular-event or invasive-cancer outcomes.
sources.limitations: Primary prevention in older adults; secondary outcomes and other populations require separate interpretation.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Vitamin D
sources.summary: Explains vitamin D status, bone health, deficiency, units and evidence on supplementation.
sources.limitations: Correcting deficiency and routinely supplementing generally healthy adults are different questions.

sources.title: LeBoff et al.: Vitamin D and incident fractures
sources.summary: In the VITAL ancillary fracture trial, vitamin D did not significantly reduce fractures in generally healthy midlife and older adults.
sources.limitations: Participants were not selected for deficiency, low bone mass or osteoporosis; this does not negate treatment for a diagnosed need.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Magnesium
sources.summary: Explains elemental magnesium, differences in salt forms, absorption, deficiency and safety.
sources.limitations: A chemical form or absorption claim alone does not prove better sleep, recovery or other clinical outcomes.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Calcium
sources.summary: Covers calcium requirements, elemental content, bone-health research and supplement considerations.
sources.limitations: Benefits depend on dietary intake and population; a larger compound mass is not necessarily more elemental calcium.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Zinc
sources.summary: Explains zinc functions, deficiency, excess intake and interactions.
sources.limitations: Evidence for one nutrient or indication does not validate a combined ZMC product.

sources.title: NIDDK: Your digestive system and how it works
sources.summary: Explains how digestion breaks proteins into amino acids and how the small intestine absorbs nutrients.
sources.limitations: Basic physiology does not establish the effectiveness of a supplement or commercial product.

sources.title: Wu et al.: Glutathione metabolism and nutritional context
sources.summary: Explains cellular synthesis from glutamate, cysteine and glycine, redox functions and the importance of adequate protein nutrition.
sources.limitations: Biological roles and disease associations do not establish that oral supplementation improves clinical outcomes.

sources.title: Richie et al.: Oral glutathione and body stores
sources.summary: A six-month placebo-controlled study in 54 healthy nonsmokers reported higher glutathione concentrations in several sampled body compartments.
sources.limitations: Biomarker changes do not establish disease prevention, a detox treatment or benefit for every formulation.

sources.title: Allen and Bradley: Oral glutathione and oxidative-stress markers
sources.summary: Forty healthy adults entered a four-week placebo-controlled study; glutathione status and measured oxidative-stress markers did not significantly improve.
sources.limitations: Short follow-up and healthy volunteers limit generalization; this trial and longer studies address different exposure periods.

sources.title: Arjinpathana and Asawanonda: Oral glutathione and skin melanin indices
sources.summary: A four-week trial in 60 healthy medical students found statistically greater melanin-index reductions than placebo at two of six measured sites.
sources.limitations: A small cosmetic study does not establish lasting skin-lightening, treatment of a pigmentation disorder or long-term safety. Published in 2012; online in 2010.

sources.title: Kusumawardani et al.: S-acetyl versus reduced glutathione for skin measures
sources.summary: A 12-week study randomized 90 women to S-acetyl glutathione, reduced glutathione or placebo. Some melanin-index analyses favored treatment, while measured pigmentation scores and blood glutathione did not differ significantly between groups.
sources.limitations: Baseline melanin indices differed; the small, selected population, short follow-up and mixed outcomes limit claims of general or lasting superiority.

sources.title: NCCIH: Melatonin, usefulness and safety
sources.summary: Distinguishes circadian uses such as jet lag from chronic insomnia, and reviews adverse effects, medicine interactions and limited long-term safety data.
sources.limitations: This US reference does not establish Indian regulatory status, prove a catalog product matches its label or support unsupervised pediatric use.

sources.title: Sletten et al.: Melatonin with behavioural scheduling for delayed sleep phase
sources.summary: A four-week trial randomized 116 clinically assessed delayed-sleep-phase patients. Melatonin combined with behavioural sleep scheduling improved sleep initiation compared with placebo and scheduling.
sources.limitations: Selected circadian-delay patients and a combined intervention; no evidence here for every sleep complaint, catalog strength or long-term treatment.

sources.title: AASM: Pharmacologic treatment guideline for chronic insomnia in adults
sources.summary: The guideline suggests against melatonin for adult sleep-onset or sleep-maintenance insomnia, reflecting weak and limited evidence for that indication.
sources.limitations: A weak recommendation addressing chronic insomnia; it is not a recommendation against all circadian-disorder uses.

sources.title: AASM: Melatonin use in children and adolescents
sources.summary: Recommends pediatric professional advice, attention to sleep habits, and keeping melatonin out of children's reach. Notes that supplement content can differ from labels.
sources.limitations: Label-variation evidence cited in the advisory is not independent testing of Indian catalog products.

sources.title: Lane and Moss: First-pass hepatic metabolism of melatonin
sources.summary: Analysis of human oral and intravenous data identified substantial liver extraction and reduced systemic availability after swallowing melatonin.
sources.limitations: An older pharmacokinetic analysis explains exposure; it does not compare modern release systems or prove clinical superiority.

sources.title: NIDDK LiverTox: Melatonin physiology
sources.summary: Describes pineal production, night-time secretion and action at melatonin receptors involved in sleep-wake regulation.
sources.limitations: Physiological signalling does not by itself establish that a supplement is necessary or effective for an individual.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Biotin, nutrition and evidence for hair claims
sources.summary: Explains biotin metabolism, rare deficiency and the limited evidence behind hair, skin and nail supplement claims.
sources.limitations: Deficiency treatment and case reports do not establish cosmetic benefits for adequately nourished consumers.

sources.title: FDA: Biotin interference with troponin laboratory tests
sources.summary: Warns that biotin can distort susceptible laboratory assays, including falsely low troponin results used in heart-attack assessment.
sources.limitations: Interference depends on the assay and exposure; the page does not provide a universal safe interval before every blood test.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Vitamin C, absorption and clinical evidence
sources.summary: Reviews dose-dependent absorption, physiological roles, cold research, adverse effects and medicine interactions.
sources.limitations: A nutrient role is not proof that a particular retail formulation prevents disease or outperforms dietary sources.

sources.title: NHS: Vitamin C, food sources and supplement cautions
sources.summary: Describes food sources, deficiency and gastrointestinal effects of excessive supplemental vitamin C.
sources.limitations: UK population guidance is not an individual prescription or evidence that Indian catalog products match their labels.

sources.title: NHS: The B-vitamin family and folic acid
sources.summary: Distinguishes individual B vitamins, their dietary roles and the risks of treating the family as one interchangeable nutrient.
sources.limitations: General dietary guidance does not diagnose the cause of fatigue or establish a need for a B-complex product.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Vitamin B12 absorption and deficiency risk
sources.summary: Explains intrinsic-factor-dependent absorption, deficiency, plant-based dietary risk, gastrointestinal causes and medicine effects.
sources.limitations: Risk factors do not diagnose deficiency; oral retail products are not a substitute for assessing absorption disorders or neurological symptoms.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Vitamin B6 and excessive-intake neuropathy
sources.summary: Reviews vitamin B6 functions, medicines and sensory-nerve injury associated with excessive supplemental exposure.
sources.limitations: Upper limits differ between authorities and are not treatment targets. Total intake from overlapping products matters.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Niacin forms and high-intake safety
sources.summary: Distinguishes nicotinic acid from nicotinamide and explains flushing, other adverse effects and medically supervised uses.
sources.limitations: Different niacin forms have different effects. Supplement pricing does not establish treatment equivalence or justify high-dose use.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Folate forms, dietary folate equivalents and safety
sources.summary: Explains food folate, folic acid and 5-MTHF; dietary folate equivalents reflect a different basis from ingredient mass.
sources.limitations: DFE conversion depends on context, and established conversion factors for supplemental 5-MTHF are lacking. Forms are not treated as identical in the catalog.

sources.title: CDC: Folic acid and prevention of neural tube defects
sources.summary: Recommends folic acid for women who could become pregnant and identifies it as the folate form shown to prevent neural tube defects.
sources.limitations: This general public-health recommendation is not an individual pregnancy plan or proof that every folate form has the same prevention evidence.

sources.title: GeneReviews: Biotinidase deficiency and targeted care
sources.summary: Describes diagnosis and specialist treatment of an inherited biotin-recycling disorder.
sources.limitations: Lifelong therapy for a diagnosed genetic disorder does not support routine high-strength biotin for cosmetic concerns.

sources.title: Hemila and Chalker: Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold
sources.summary: Placebo-controlled trial synthesis found no general-population reduction in cold incidence, with modestly shorter colds during regular supplementation.
sources.limitations: Trials differ in population and protocol; these findings do not establish prevention by every formulation or benefit from starting after symptoms begin.

sources.title: Viribay et al.: Arginine and exercise-performance meta-analysis
sources.summary: A 2020 synthesis reported pooled performance improvements across selected arginine trials.
sources.limitations: Protocols and participants differed, aerobic results were heterogeneous, and a 2025 commentary identified calculation and analysis problems. Read the commentary and authors' reply alongside the original.

sources.title: Trexler: Methodological critique of the arginine meta-analysis
sources.summary: Identifies potential errors involving outliers, standard errors versus standard deviations, mixed effect-size methods and dependent outcomes in the 2020 analysis.
sources.limitations: A critique of one synthesis, not a new randomized trial or proof that every possible arginine use is ineffective.

sources.title: Viribay et al.: Reply to the arginine meta-analysis critique
sources.summary: The authors acknowledge the importance of the identified data-handling problems and describe improved approaches in subsequent work.
sources.limitations: The reply does not supply a corrected pooled arginine-performance estimate that resolves the original result.

sources.title: Schulman et al.: VINTAGE MI arginine trial after heart attack
sources.summary: A trial of 153 patients following acute myocardial infarction found no improvement in the measured vascular or cardiac outcomes and raised a mortality safety concern.
sources.limitations: A specific post-heart-attack population; this does not quantify risk for healthy athletes, but it argues against unsupervised post-infarction use.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Carnitine, nutritional roles and supplement evidence
sources.summary: Explains endogenous synthesis, mitochondrial fatty-acid transport, deficiency states, mixed clinical findings and gastrointestinal, medication and other safety considerations.
sources.limitations: The physiological role is not proof of fat loss from a retail supplement. Clinical uses and healthy-adult sports marketing address different questions.

sources.title: L-carnitine and body composition: 37-trial meta-analysis
sources.summary: The 2020 analysis found a small average reduction in body weight, with no significant change in waist circumference or body-fat percentage overall.
sources.limitations: Results vary across participants and protocols and do not demonstrate rapid fat burning, a guaranteed response or superiority of a branded form.

sources.title: Jackman et al.: BCAA and acute post-exercise muscle protein synthesis
sources.summary: In ten resistance-trained young men, BCAA increased an acute muscle-protein-synthesis measure compared with a placebo after resistance exercise.
sources.limitations: An acute physiological endpoint with a placebo comparator; this does not establish long-term muscle gain, superiority to complete protein or benefit on top of an adequate diet.

sources.title: Kaspy et al.: BCAA signalling and muscle-protein turnover
sources.summary: BCAA can stimulate signalling and transient protein synthesis, but the synthesis response is smaller than that observed with a complete protein supplying all indispensable amino acids.
sources.limitations: A narrative review of physiological studies; a signal or short-term synthesis change does not establish improved long-term performance. Published in 2024, online in 2023.

sources.title: Ferrando et al.: ISSN essential-amino-acid position stand
sources.summary: Reviews how all nine essential amino acids support muscle-protein synthesis and potential uses in exercise, ageing and selected clinical or low-intake settings.
sources.limitations: A position statement rather than a brand comparison. Acute synthesis findings are not equivalent to long-term strength gains; read the disclosed commercial relationships and patents.

sources.title: Harty et al.: Multi-ingredient pre-workout evidence and safety
sources.summary: Some tested blends improved selected endurance, mood or training outcomes, while findings for force and power were mixed. Undisclosed ingredient amounts make comparison difficult.
sources.limitations: Formulas differ substantially and most safety studies were shorter than eight weeks. Results for a tested blend do not validate every pre-workout or establish long-term safety.

sources.title: Guest et al.: ISSN caffeine and exercise-performance position stand
sources.summary: Caffeine can improve some exercise outcomes, especially endurance, but responses differ and adverse effects can include disturbed sleep and anxiety.
sources.limitations: Evidence for caffeine does not establish that every multi-ingredient product is effective or appropriate. Read the authors' disclosed commercial relationships.

sources.title: American Academy of Pediatrics: Dry scooping and pre-workout risks
sources.summary: Explains choking and inhalation risks from swallowing dry powder, caffeine concerns, and why pre-workout products are inappropriate shortcuts for young athletes.
sources.limitations: US pediatric guidance does not establish Indian regulatory status or the contents of a particular catalog product.

sources.title: Linus Pauling Institute: Carnitine metabolism and forms
sources.summary: Describes synthesis, intestinal absorption, kidney conservation and the mitochondrial carnitine shuttle, and distinguishes L-carnitine from its derivatives.
sources.limitations: Last scientific review shown is December 2019. Physiological and absorption differences do not establish a retail product's clinical superiority. Supplement and prescribed-treatment contexts differ.

sources.title: Gwin et al.: EAA-enriched whey during an energy deficit
sources.summary: Ten young adults completed a crossover study of short-term energy deficits. EAA-enriched whey improved acute whole-body protein balance relative to comparators, while measured mixed-muscle protein synthesis did not differ.
sources.limitations: A small, acute study in a specific underfeeding setting, using an EAA-plus-whey blend. It does not demonstrate extra long-term muscle gain from every EAA-only product.

sources.title: Wang et al.: Citrulline malate exercise-performance synthesis
sources.summary: A June 2026 synthesis of 30 trials and 644 participants found a small pooled performance effect and no significant pooled improvement in perceived exertion.
sources.limitations: Certainty was low to very low, prediction intervals were wide and subgroup findings were not robust. It does not establish reliable timing, amounts or universal benefit.

sources.title: Malate or not? L-citrulline versus citrulline malate
sources.summary: A crossover trial in 43 trained adults compared placebo with L-citrulline and citrulline malate matched for delivered citrulline; the tested neuromuscular outcomes did not clearly improve.
sources.limitations: A specific acute protocol cannot settle every use, but it does not demonstrate an added performance advantage from malate. Published online in December 2024.

sources.title: A critical review of citrulline malate and exercise performance
sources.summary: Examines proposed arginine/nitric-oxide mechanisms, mixed exercise findings and the difficulty of interpreting citrulline-malate composition.
sources.limitations: Mechanisms and nominal ratios do not establish delivered L-citrulline, clinical equivalence or product superiority.

sources.title: Trexler et al.: ISSN beta-alanine position stand
sources.summary: Repeated beta-alanine use can increase muscle carnosine, with potential benefits for particular high-intensity exercise tasks. Paraesthesia is a recognized effect.
sources.limitations: An older position statement; effects depend on the activity and exposure period, and do not establish universal strength, muscle-gain or endurance benefits. Read commercial disclosures.

sources.title: Saunders et al.: Beta-alanine exercise meta-analysis
sources.summary: Synthesizes exercise capacity and performance trials, finding a small overall benefit with meaningful differences between exercise tests and task durations.
sources.limitations: Capacity tests and competitive performance are different outcomes; a pooled effect does not establish benefit for every athlete or sport.

sources.title: Dolan et al.: Beta-alanine safety assessment
sources.summary: Across available studies, tingling was the principal reported side effect; dropout rates were similar to placebo and human muscle taurine did not show a significant reduction.
sources.limitations: Safety conclusions apply to studied exposures and participants. Sparse long-term or special-population data should not be treated as proof of unlimited safety.

sources.title: Kurtz et al.: Taurine in sports and exercise
sources.summary: Reviews isolated taurine, gastrointestinal uptake, tissue and kidney regulation, and proposed calcium-handling and exercise mechanisms. Performance and recovery findings were mixed.
sources.limitations: Many proposed pathways rely on preclinical work; studies of isolated taurine cannot establish the benefit or safety of a caffeinated energy-drink blend.

sources.title: Deng et al.: Acute taurine exercise meta-analysis
sources.summary: A 2025 review of 23 randomized trials reported a small overall exercise effect, with inconsistent findings across tasks and sensitivity analyses.
sources.limitations: Evidence certainty was low to very low, and prediction intervals often included no effect. These short studies do not establish universal or long-term benefits.

sources.title: Zawieja et al.: Chronic betaine and exercise performance
sources.summary: Seventeen studies involving 317 participants showed a pooled maximal-strength benefit, especially in lower-body measures, but not consistent improvements in upper-body strength, cycling sprint power or muscular endurance.
sources.limitations: Small studies and different outcomes limit certainty. Anhydrous betaine findings do not establish digestive benefits for betaine hydrochloride.

sources.title: Betaine and endurance performance: a systematic review
sources.summary: A 2025 synthesis found only five eligible endurance studies and judged all to have high risk of bias. Some outcomes improved, but the overall evidence remained inconclusive.
sources.limitations: Sparse heterogeneous studies do not identify a dependable endurance benefit or prove that a change in a physiological marker improves sport performance.

sources.title: Yago et al.: Betaine HCl and experimentally raised gastric pH
sources.summary: A small healthy-volunteer experiment found that betaine hydrochloride temporarily lowered gastric pH after acid-suppressing medication had raised it.
sources.limitations: An experimentally induced pH change is not proof of improved digestion, symptom relief, a diagnosis of low stomach acid or improved exercise performance.

sources.title: EMA: Betaine anhydrous in specialist homocystinuria care
sources.summary: Explains betaine-mediated conversion of homocysteine to methionine and its use alongside other treatment in a specific inherited disease. Specialist monitoring is required.
sources.limitations: A European medicine assessment, not a recommendation for a retail workout product, Indian regulatory guidance or evidence that healthy people need supplementation.

sources.title: Rathmacher et al.: Updated ISSN HMB position stand
sources.summary: Reviews HMB as a leucine metabolite, calcium and free-acid forms, protein-turnover mechanisms and studies in varied training and clinical settings.
sources.limitations: Its conclusions differ from some meta-analyses. Read population-specific results and the authors' disclosed industry affiliations and commercial relationships. Published online in December 2024, in the 2025 volume.

sources.title: Jakubowski et al.: HMB with resistance training in younger adults
sources.summary: The 2020 analysis found no additional overall improvements in body composition or strength from HMB alongside resistance training in adults aged 18 to 45.
sources.limitations: Study selection and methods have been debated. These results do not settle every clinical or nutritional context, and they do not test every commercial formulation.

sources.title: Wang et al.: HMB as an adjunct to training in older adults
sources.summary: Published in April 2026, this synthesis of 13 trials and 561 participants found no overall added improvement in muscle mass, fat mass or strength in adults aged 50 and over.
sources.limitations: Health status, interventions and strength outcomes differed across trials. A pooled result in people undertaking exercise cannot be generalized to every patient with malnutrition or immobility.

sources.title: NHS: The Eatwell Guide and ordinary protein foods
sources.summary: Identifies pulses, fish, eggs, meat and dairy foods within a varied dietary pattern.
sources.limitations: UK population food guidance; examples do not specify an individual's protein needs or Indian product composition.

sources.title: NHS: Vegetarian diet and protein variety
sources.summary: Explains vegetarian protein foods, including pulses, tofu, eggs and dairy, and the role of dietary variety.
sources.limitations: A general dietary overview, not a comparison of commercial isolates or a measured nutrient analysis of every preparation.

sources.title: NIDDK: Healthy eating for adults with chronic kidney disease
sources.summary: Explains why protein, mineral and fluid choices in kidney disease need an individualized nutrition plan.
sources.limitations: Kidney-disease guidance must not be extrapolated into a claim that ordinary protein intake harms healthy kidneys.

sources.title: FDA: Food allergies, ingredient identification and avoidance
sources.summary: Identifies major food allergens and the importance of recognizing allergenic ingredients, including milk-derived whey.
sources.limitations: US labelling law is not an assertion about Indian regulatory compliance; check each actual product and individual allergy advice.

sources.title: NCCIH: Omega-3 foods, supplements and clinical limits
sources.summary: Distinguishes seafood EPA/DHA from plant ALA and reviews supplement evidence and safety concerns.
sources.limitations: Food examples do not assign a supplement-equivalent amount; prescription therapies and ordinary retail fish oil are distinct contexts.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Vitamin D foods and fortified products
sources.summary: Explains naturally occurring food sources, variable fortification, mushroom vitamin D and the need to check product labels.
sources.limitations: Food examples are not standardized treatment doses. Fortification practices described in the US are not assumed for Indian milk or plant drinks.

sources.title: Health Canada: Ordinary protein foods in a varied diet
sources.summary: Lists beans, lentils, soy foods, eggs, fish, poultry, nuts, seeds and dairy as protein foods, and notes the need for reliable fortified B12 sources in a plant-only diet.
sources.limitations: Food examples support adequate protein nutrition; the guidance does not measure glutathione precursor doses or prove that a food is clinically equivalent to a glutathione supplement.

sources.title: Burkhardt et al.: Melatonin measured in two tart-cherry cultivars
sources.summary: Laboratory analysis detected melatonin in fresh-frozen Montmorency and Balaton tart cherries, with different concentrations between the cultivars.
sources.limitations: An analysis of particular fruit samples does not establish predictable content in all cherries, a supplement-equivalent intake or clinical treatment of insomnia.

sources.title: FDA: Dietary protein, amino acids and food sources
sources.summary: Lists animal and plant protein foods and explains complete and complementary amino-acid profiles.
sources.limitations: Used for food-source context, not a personalized intake plan, an amino-acid supplement prescription or evidence that every Indian diet is adequate.

sources.title: MedlinePlus: Essential amino acids and dietary variety
sources.summary: Explains the nine essential amino acids, protein digestion and the value of dietary variety over the day.
sources.limitations: Does not compare supplement brands, establish an intake gap or require complementary plant foods to be paired at one meal.

sources.title: Collins et al.: Watermelon as a dietary citrulline source
sources.summary: A controlled feeding study used watermelon juice as a natural citrulline source and measured circulating amino-acid responses.
sources.limitations: A biomarker study, not proof of improved exercise performance. Ordinary fruit or juice is not assumed to match an isolated L-citrulline or citrulline-malate serving.

sources.title: Wu: Food taurine, creatine and carnosine composition
sources.summary: Describes taurine and beta-alanine-containing dipeptides such as carnosine and anserine in animal-source foods.
sources.limitations: Used here only for food composition and molecular-form distinctions. The article's broader health claims are not adopted as proof of routine supplement need, disease prevention or vegetarian-diet deficiency.

sources.title: USDA ARS: Betaine concentrations in common foods
sources.summary: Identifies dietary betaine sources including wheat bran, wheat germ, spinach and beets from food-composition analysis.
sources.limitations: Older US composition research is used qualitatively; no food amounts, Indian cultivar values, exercise benefits or betaine-HCl equivalence are inferred.

sources.title: NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians: common vitamin C food sources
sources.summary: The National Institute of Nutrition identifies amla and guava among vitamin C food sources familiar in India.
sources.limitations: An older dietary manual, used here only for qualitative food-source examples. It is not the source of current clinical dosing recommendations; food content varies with variety, storage and preparation.

sources.title: USDA National Nutrient Database, Standard Reference 28
sources.summary: Published composition per 100 g edible food; NDB identifiers are retained with each food.
sources.limitations: Reference composition, not a test of an Indian recipe, brand or portion. Cooking, cultivar and fortification change amounts.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Thiamin
sources.summary: Adult reference intakes and deficiency context for this individual B vitamin.
sources.limitations: General reference; individual needs and food composition vary. This is not an India-specific prescription.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Riboflavin
sources.summary: Adult reference intakes and deficiency context for this individual B vitamin.
sources.limitations: General reference; individual needs and food composition vary. This is not an India-specific prescription.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Pantothenic acid
sources.summary: Adult reference intakes and deficiency context for this individual B vitamin.
sources.limitations: General reference; individual needs and food composition vary. This is not an India-specific prescription.

sources.title: FDA: caffeine and adult consumption
sources.summary: General adult caffeine benchmark; sensitivity, medicines and health context can require less.
sources.limitations: General reference; individual needs and food composition vary. This is not an India-specific prescription.

sources.title: ADA Standards of Care 2026: nutrition and health behaviours
sources.summary: Individualized nutrition is part of diabetes care; it does not establish protein powder as a diabetes treatment.
sources.limitations: General reference; individual needs and food composition vary. This is not an India-specific prescription.

sources.title: Creatine and Parkinson disease: NET-PD randomized trial
sources.summary: The large trial did not show slowed clinical progression and was stopped for futility.
sources.limitations: Parkinson disease trial; findings do not resolve every cognitive question or establish treatment for another neurological condition.

sources.title: Chicken breast bioactive compounds during refrigerated storage
sources.summary: Primary laboratory measurements of creatine and carnosine in raw chicken breast, with the farm and storage day specified.
sources.limitations: Study-specific Korean broiler samples, not universal Indian chicken composition; cooking and storage change amounts.

sources.title: NIH ODS: supplement labels, quality testing and claims
sources.summary: Explains labels, third-party quality testing and the distinction between composition checks and clinical safety or effectiveness.
sources.limitations: US consumer guidance; this does not certify any Indian catalog product or establish batch-specific testing.

sources.title: Reactome: Human glutathione peroxidase reaction
sources.summary: Curated human GPX2 reaction showing reduced glutathione consumption during peroxide reduction and formation of oxidised glutathione; includes underlying experimental references.
sources.limitations: A biochemical reaction annotation, not evidence that oral glutathione products improve clinical outcomes. The selected record describes GPX2; related glutathione peroxidases have distinct locations and substrates.

sources.title: Reactome: Human glutathione reductase and NADPH recycling
sources.summary: Curated human cytosolic reaction showing glutathione reductase using NADPH to convert oxidised glutathione into reduced glutathione; includes underlying experimental references.
sources.limitations: A cellular recycling reaction, not a measure of oral bioavailability, product quality or supplementation benefit.

sources.title: Lambert: Taurine transport and cellular volume regulation
sources.summary: Describes taurine as an organic osmolyte and the regulation of cellular taurine uptake and release during osmotic volume changes.
sources.limitations: Mechanistic synthesis involving cell models; it does not establish that an oral taurine product improves hydration, exercise performance or health outcomes in humans.

sources.title: Breksa and Garrow: Human betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase
sources.summary: Describes the human enzyme that transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine, forming dimethylglycine and methionine, and its expression in liver and kidney.
sources.limitations: A biochemical study using recombinant human enzyme, not a supplementation trial. The mechanism does not establish a benefit from extra betaine or justify independent treatment of a medical condition.

sources.title: Antonio et al.: One-year higher-protein crossover study in trained men
sources.summary: A small study alternating habitual and higher-protein dietary periods reported no adverse changes in measured kidney, liver or lipid markers in resistance-trained men.
sources.limitations: Fourteen men completed the study. Routine blood markers, a selected healthy population and a limited follow-up cannot establish lifetime safety, safety in kidney disease or safety at any possible intake.

sources.title: Hevia-Larrain et al.: Protein-matched vegan and omnivorous diets during training
sources.summary: Habitual vegans and omnivores completed supervised resistance training while protein intake was matched using soy or whey supplementation. Both groups improved with no detected between-group differences in measured muscle and strength outcomes.
sources.limitations: Thirty-eight untrained young men; participants were already vegan or omnivorous rather than randomly assigned to those diets. The result concerns adequate total intake and these diets, not every isolated serving or product.

sources.title: Gorissen et al.: Amino-acid composition of commercial protein ingredients
sources.summary: Measured amino-acid composition across plant and animal protein ingredients, finding important differences among sources and within the plant category.
sources.limitations: A composition analysis, not a digestibility or long-term training trial. Tryptophan was not measured. Tested ingredients cannot certify all finished products or every later batch.

sources.title: Trommelen et al.: Larger protein feeding and prolonged post-exercise response
sources.summary: In young men studied after exercise, a 100-gram milk-protein feeding produced a larger and more prolonged anabolic response than 25 grams during a 12-hour observation period.
sources.limitations: An acute study with specific amounts, protein and participants; it does not establish an unlimited response, optimal meal distribution, long-term superiority or an individual serving recommendation. Read the disclosed dairy-industry relationships.

sources.title: Schoenfeld et al.: Protein immediately before versus after resistance training
sources.summary: Twenty-one trained men took an equal protein supplement before or after resistance training for ten weeks, with similar measured changes in strength, hypertrophy and body composition.
sources.limitations: Small trial with no unsupplemented comparison. It challenges a narrow timing rule but cannot prove timing never matters across meal patterns, ages or clinical circumstances. The paper has a published correction.

sources.title: Evenepoel et al.: Human digestibility of cooked versus raw egg protein
sources.summary: In a crossover experiment, cooked egg protein had substantially greater measured ileal digestibility than the same test meal in raw form.
sources.limitations: Five participants with ileostomies and specific test meals. The results do not describe every cooking method, commercial egg powder or other protein ingredient.

sources.title: Van Lieshout et al.: Milk-protein glycation and lysine availability in humans
sources.summary: In healthy young men, experimentally high glycation of milk protein reduced the post-meal appearance of protein-derived lysine compared with a low-glycation preparation.
sources.limitations: An acute study of deliberately contrasting processing conditions, not proof that normal home cooking destroys protein or a test of every finished supplement. Several authors disclosed dairy-industry employment or research relationships.

sources.title: Nabuco et al.: Whey and resistance training in older women
sources.summary: Older women assigned whey before or after resistance training had greater improvements in measured muscle mass, strength and walking performance than the placebo group during the training programme.
sources.limitations: A 12-week study in preconditioned older women, not a prediction of an individual's appearance or an indication that all women require protein supplements.

sources.title: Van Vliet et al.: Whole eggs versus protein-matched egg whites after exercise
sources.summary: Whole eggs stimulated a greater acute post-exercise myofibrillar protein-synthesis response than equal-protein egg whites in young men, despite similar total leucine availability.
sources.limitations: The meals differed in fat and energy as well as food matrix. An acute comparison of two egg meals does not establish that all whole foods outperform shakes or predict long-term hypertrophy.

sources.title: US Dairy Export Council: Whey and lactose ingredient reference manual
sources.summary: Defines whey ingredient categories and describes manufacturing and typical composition, including the generally lower lactose and higher protein concentration of isolate ingredients.
sources.limitations: A dairy-industry technical publication, not an independent clinical comparison or a test of Indian finished products. Ingredient specifications and typical values do not certify a flavoured product or justify assuming zero lactose.

sources.title: Lockwood et al.: Hydrolysed whey and concentrate variants during resistance training
sources.summary: Compared extensively hydrolysed whey, two concentrate preparations and carbohydrate placebo during eight weeks of resistance training. Strength increases were similar between groups; selected body-composition results differed.
sources.limitations: College-aged men, specific preparations and an eight-week programme. This was not a head-to-head isolate versus concentrate trial and does not establish a universal processing hierarchy. The paper was published online in 2016 and in its journal issue in 2017; authors included commercial affiliations.

sources.title: Boirie et al.: Slow and fast milk proteins in human protein metabolism
sources.summary: Whey and casein produced different time courses of amino-acid availability and whole-body protein synthesis and breakdown after single meals in healthy adults.
sources.limitations: Acute whole-body protein handling, not a long-term training comparison or proof that every casein ingredient, mixed meal or night-time product behaves identically.

sources.title: Babault et al.: Pea, whey and placebo during upper-limb training
sources.summary: A 12-week study in young men compared a specific pea protein with whey and placebo. No difference was detected between the two protein groups; favourable pea-versus-placebo thickness findings were clearest in a weaker-participant subgroup.
sources.limitations: The overall between-group muscle-thickness test did not reach conventional statistical significance, strength changes did not differ between groups, and subgroup findings require care. The study involved a branded ingredient and manufacturer-affiliated authors.

sources.title: Joy et al.: Rice versus whey protein during eight weeks of training
sources.summary: Compared large, equal-protein rice and whey isolate servings during resistance training in young trained men, without detected between-group differences in measured body-composition or performance adaptations.
sources.limitations: Small sample, short follow-up and large test servings. Failure to detect a difference is not a formal equivalence result and cannot establish interchangeability at all serving sizes or for every rice ingredient.

sources.title: Briskey et al.: A specific yeast protein during resistance training
sources.summary: An eight-week trial compared an extracted Saccharomyces cerevisiae protein ingredient, whey and maltodextrin alongside resistance exercise, reporting selected lean-mass and performance changes and analyses in participants with lower protein intake.
sources.limitations: Manufacturer-funded, ingredient-specific study with multiple outcomes and subgroup analyses. It does not establish equivalence for all yeast products, distinguish every preparation's digestibility or validate nutritional yeast as the same intervention.

sources.title: Bai et al.: Six-month whey and yeast supplementation study in older adults
sources.summary: A 2026 trial compared whey protein, yeast protein and a control group over six months in Chinese older adults, assessing muscle mass, strength, function and other measures.
sources.limitations: Specific preparations and an older-adult population; findings cannot establish category-wide equivalence or superiority for athletes, every yeast species or all commercial powders. Trial populations excluded several significant medical conditions.

sources.title: Van der Heijden et al.: Algal preparations and acute muscle protein synthesis
sources.summary: Protein-matched spirulina, chlorella and mycoprotein feedings increased myofibrillar protein synthesis over four hours in young adults, with no detected group difference despite differing amino-acid time courses.
sources.limitations: An acute study of specific preparations, with mycoprotein as comparator rather than whey. It does not establish long-term hypertrophy, equivalence of all algal products or adequate protein delivery from a small greens serving.

sources.title: Williamson et al.: Species and processing differences in algal amino-acid availability
sources.summary: Ten young adults consumed protein-matched milk, spirulina, whole-cell chlorella and split-cell chlorella drinks. Post-meal amino-acid availability differed substantially among preparations.
sources.limitations: Small acute study with carbohydrate-containing drinks, not long-term training or a universal digestibility ranking. The split-cell versus whole-cell difference was not conventionally significant, so processing superiority must not be asserted from this trial alone.

sources.title: Antonio et al.: Common creatine questions and misconceptions
sources.summary: Explains distinctions between creatine and anabolic steroids, creatine and creatinine, and evidence on common safety and efficacy claims.
sources.limitations: A narrative expert review rather than a new trial; several authors disclose supplement-industry relationships. Later topic-specific trials should also be considered.

sources.title: Powers et al.: Creatine, total body water and fluid distribution
sources.summary: In 32 resistance-trained men and women, the tested monohydrate protocol increased body mass and total body water without changing relative fluid distribution.
sources.limitations: A small, short-term study. Water-related mass changes do not quantify fat gain, permanent bloating or every individual's response.

sources.title: Creatine and hair loss: 12-week placebo-controlled trial
sources.summary: The 2025 trial directly assessed androgens and hair measures in resistance-trained men. Among 38 completers, with hair data for 37, it found no supplement-related effect on measured hair outcomes or DHT.
sources.limitations: Small sample of men and 12-week exposure; it cannot exclude every long-term effect or individual susceptibility. Authors disclose relevant commercial advisory or research relationships.

sources.title: Lugaresi et al.: Creatine and measured kidney filtration
sources.summary: A 12-week placebo-controlled trial in resistance-trained adults eating a high-protein diet found no impairment of directly measured glomerular filtration with the tested creatine protocol.
sources.limitations: Small study of healthy participants. Its findings do not establish safety in kidney disease, unexplained abnormal renal tests, every medication context or unlimited dosing.

sources.title: Hultman et al.: Muscle creatine loading in men
sources.summary: Muscle-biopsy measurements showed that a lower daily intake increased muscle creatine more gradually over 28 days, reaching a similar eventual increase to a rapid loading approach.
sources.limitations: Study in men with particular regimens and biochemical outcomes. It supports the distinction between loading speed and eventual storage, not an individualized dosing prescription.

sources.title: Creatine timing: Eight-week trial in collegiate athletes
sources.summary: Compared pre-training creatine, post-training creatine and placebo over eight weeks in 34 resistance-trained male and female athletes; no clear pre-versus-post advantage was established.
sources.limitations: Small groups and short duration; an absence of a statistically detected difference is not proof of equivalence for every timing regimen or population.

sources.title: Creatine and cognitive performance: Preregistered crossover trial
sources.summary: A double-blind crossover trial with 123 participants found at most a small possible cognitive effect; key outcomes were not conventionally significant and exploratory tasks did not improve.
sources.limitations: Does not settle effects in every population, cognitive domain or condition such as sleep deprivation, and does not establish treatment of a cognitive disorder.

sources.title: Watson et al.: Creatine and exercise heat tolerance
sources.summary: Short-term monohydrate did not compromise hydration status or temperature regulation in trained men tested during exercise in heat after dehydration.
sources.limitations: Small, short-term study in trained men under a specified protocol; it does not remove the risks of dehydration or heat illness or define a universal fluid requirement.

sources.title: Creatine compounds: Chemistry, bioavailability and evidence review
sources.summary: Reviews creatine compounds, theoretical creatine fractions by molecular mass, bioavailability requirements, delivery formats and evidence needed for claims about novel forms.
sources.limitations: Narrative review with disclosed commercial relationships. Molecular fractions are theoretical composition values, not potency or absorption percentages, and the review does not verify a particular retail batch.

sources.title: Fast-dissolving creatine monohydrate: Formulation methods
sources.summary: Reviews physical and chemical formulation techniques, including particle-size reduction, and their effects on dissolution and material properties.
sources.limitations: Formulation and patent evidence is not equivalent to head-to-head human performance evidence. Processing claims cannot be generalized to every finished product carrying a micronized label.

sources.title: Creatine HCl versus monohydrate: Eight-week training trial
sources.summary: Compared HCl, monohydrate with or without loading, and placebo alongside eight weeks of training in 40 men. It did not establish a clear HCl advantage.
sources.limitations: Ten participants per group, male sample, no muscle-creatine measurements and indirect body-composition estimates. Not an equivalence trial or proof that every small HCl serving replaces a studied monohydrate regimen.

sources.title: Galvan et al.: Creatine nitrate safety and performance trials
sources.summary: Acute and 28-day trials measured nitrate protocols, exercise outcomes and muscle creatine. Some bench-press findings favoured the higher nitrate protocol, while only monohydrate retained a significant muscle-creatine increase at day 28.
sources.limitations: Short duration, modest sample sizes, formulation-specific amounts and multiple outcomes. Does not establish nitrate's universal superiority, long-term safety or equivalence across delivered creatine amounts; commercial involvement is disclosed.

sources.title: Jagim et al.: Buffered creatine versus monohydrate
sources.summary: The tested buffered formulation did not produce greater muscle-creatine changes, body-composition changes or training adaptations than monohydrate over 28 days.
sources.limitations: One buffered preparation, modest sample and short study period. Findings do not certify all buffered products or prove all formulations are interchangeable; supplement-related funding and relationships should be read.

sources.title: Spillane et al.: Creatine ethyl ester versus monohydrate
sources.summary: Seven-week trial in 30 men found no ethyl-ester advantage for strength or body composition, lower muscle-creatine gains than monohydrate, and higher serum creatinine.
sources.limitations: Small study in previously untrained men with a specified ester preparation. A serum-creatinine increase is not, by itself, a diagnosis of kidney injury or a finding about every creatine product.

sources.title: Pereira et al.: Creatine gummies in female beach-volleyball athletes
sources.summary: A 10-week study in 32 female beach-volleyball athletes found improved jump and change-of-direction outcomes with one monohydrate gummy preparation compared with no supplementation.
sources.limitations: No placebo or powder comparator, small sport-specific sample, donated products and disclosed industry advisory relationships. It does not establish a gummy-format advantage, all-brand label accuracy or finished-product shelf stability.

sources.title: Ganguly et al.: Stability of dissolved effervescent creatine
sources.summary: Measured concentration changes, degradation and crystallization during prolonged storage of a dissolved effervescent creatine preparation at specified temperatures.
sources.limitations: An aqueous preparation tested under particular laboratory conditions, not a gummy-matrix study. Its numerical degradation rates cannot be transferred to every drink, gummy, jelly or dry product.

sources.title: Iwai et al.: Collagen-derived peptides in human blood after gelatin hydrolysates
sources.summary: Identified small hydroxyproline-containing peptides, especially proline-hydroxyproline, in circulation after adults ingested gelatin hydrolysates from specified animal sources.
sources.limitations: A study of digestion and circulating peptides, not proof of intact collagen delivery to joints or skin, tissue repair or a clinical supplement benefit.

sources.title: Paul et al.: Collagen peptides and indispensable amino-acid balance
sources.summary: Describes collagen's incomplete indispensable amino-acid pattern, including lack of tryptophan, and models how it can fit within a specified mixed dietary pattern.
sources.limitations: Industry-associated modelling of a Western diet, not a muscle-growth trial or proof of an appropriate replacement fraction for every person's diet. The model does not make collagen alone equivalent to complete protein.

sources.title: Oikawa et al.: Whey versus collagen peptides and muscle protein synthesis in older women
sources.summary: Twenty-two older women received whey or collagen peptides during a six-day protocol. Whey produced greater acute and integrated muscle-protein-synthesis responses with and without the exercise intervention.
sources.limitations: Small, short study in older women; synthesis measures do not establish a universal long-term muscle-size ranking or treatment of sarcopenia. A published corrigendum should be read with the original paper.

sources.title: Lugo et al.: Undenatured type II collagen and knee osteoarthritis symptoms
sources.summary: A 180-day trial in 191 people with knee osteoarthritis compared a particular undenatured type II ingredient with placebo and glucosamine plus chondroitin, reporting favourable symptom-score changes with the tested ingredient.
sources.limitations: Sponsored by the ingredient supplier, with company-affiliated authors. Product-specific symptom results do not establish cartilage regrowth, a proven human immune mechanism or equivalence of other collagen preparations.

sources.title: Shaw et al.: Vitamin C-enriched gelatin before intermittent activity
sources.summary: Eight healthy men consumed vitamin C-containing gelatin preparations before brief exercise. The study assessed circulating amino acids, a collagen-synthesis marker and effects of participant serum in a laboratory ligament model.
sources.limitations: Small mechanistic experiment with surrogate outcomes and an ex vivo model; it did not demonstrate healed human tendons, fewer injuries, a universal timing rule or an isolated effect of extra vitamin C.

sources.title: Lis and Baar: Different vitamin C-enriched collagen derivatives before exercise
sources.summary: Ten recreationally active men consumed matched gelatin, hydrolysed collagen, a mixed gummy or placebo before brief activity. Amino acids rose, while variability prevented statistically significant treatment effects on the measured collagen-synthesis marker.
sources.limitations: Small acute experiment, not a trial of injury recovery or long-term tendon function. Trends and increased amino-acid availability do not establish a clinical benefit or superiority of one delivery format.

sources.title: Myung and Park: Collagen supplements and skin aging, with funding and quality analyses
sources.summary: Across 23 randomized trials, pooled skin outcomes favoured supplementation, but effects did not persist in independently funded or higher-quality study subgroups, leading the authors to question routine anti-aging recommendations.
sources.limitations: The search ended in June 2024, subgroup comparisons have limited power and are not randomized comparisons of funding. Later syntheses use different studies and methods; disagreement should remain visible.

sources.title: Oral collagen peptides and skin rejuvenation: Updated meta-analysis of randomized trials
sources.summary: A July 2026 synthesis of 35 randomized trials reported benefits for hydration, elasticity and barrier measures, with less certain effects on wrinkles and structural skin outcomes.
sources.limitations: Formulations, methods and study durations differ; the paper's treatment of bias and pooled outcomes should be considered alongside conflicting reviews. A pooled cosmetic outcome does not certify every product or establish prevention of skin disease.

sources.title: Hydrolyzed collagen for skin aging: Methodological critique and reanalysis
sources.summary: An October 2026 methodological analysis questions data extraction, outcome compatibility and bias in collagen skin meta-analyses and argues that corrected evidence does not support validated anti-aging treatment claims.
sources.limitations: A critical reanalysis rather than a new randomized clinical trial. Its conclusion conflicts with favourable syntheses and depends on analytical choices and the available underlying studies.

sources.title: Alcock et al.: Variability of collagen-related amino acids in bone broth
sources.summary: Analysed commercial and laboratory bone broths, finding marked recipe-dependent variation in collagen-related amino acids and lower amounts in some standardized preparations than the reference supplement exposure.
sources.limitations: Preparation-specific amino-acid analysis, not universal collagen grams per cup, a clinical outcome trial or proof that every broth is nutritionally equivalent to a collagen supplement.

sources.title: Collagen supplementation for joint health: Composition and proposed mechanisms
sources.summary: Distinguishes native collagen, gelatin and hydrolysed preparations, including the proposed oral-tolerance rationale for native type II and digestion-related hypotheses for hydrolysates.
sources.limitations: A review involving supplement-industry affiliations, drawing partly on preclinical mechanisms. Proposed immune or peptide pathways are not established causal explanations of benefits in every human user or formulation.

sources.title: VA/DoD: 2026 hip and knee osteoarthritis patient guidance
sources.summary: Explains osteoarthritis management using individualized activity, weight management where relevant, rehabilitation and symptom treatment; states that evidence is insufficient for dietary supplements as effective OA treatment.
sources.limitations: US VA/DoD guidance, not an Indian treatment protocol or a direct evaluation of every collagen ingredient. It supports maintaining established care and avoiding claims that oral supplements cure osteoarthritis.

sources.title: Jerger et al.: Specific collagen peptides and intramuscular collagen during training
sources.summary: Twenty-nine men completed 12 weeks of high-load resistance training with a specific collagen-peptide preparation or placebo. The supplement group had a greater increase in intramuscular collagen type I content; type III and IV changes did not differ between groups.
sources.limitations: Small ingredient-specific study with a tissue-structure outcome rather than clinical tendon healing or equivalence to whey. Commercial support and a co-author's collagen-related patents and honoraria require consideration.

sources.title: Churchward-Venne et al.: Low-dose whey with leucine or essential amino acids
sources.summary: Compared a small whey serving enriched with leucine or other essential amino acids against a larger complete-whey treatment, measuring muscle protein synthesis at rest and after exercise.
sources.limitations: Acute study in men using specified mixtures. It is not a long-term training trial or a demonstration that every leucine, BCAA or EAA product is interchangeable. Read the original funding and commercial disclosures.

sources.title: Alcock et al.: Amino-acid exposure after dairy and collagen proteins
sources.summary: Characterized the amino-acid content and post-meal blood responses to specified dairy and collagen proteins and a bone-broth serving in active men.
sources.limitations: Acute exposure and specific foods/preparations. It does not establish long-term clinical outcomes or a universal amount of collagen in homemade broth; portions and amino-acid profiles are not identical.

sources.title: Shaw et al.: Vitamin-C-enriched gelatin and a collagen-formation marker
sources.summary: Eight men completed a gelatin-plus-vitamin-C and intermittent-exercise experiment. Blood amino acids and a type I collagen-formation marker were assessed; participant serum was also applied to engineered ligaments.
sources.limitations: Very small study. The blood marker is not direct tendon or cartilage synthesis, the engineered-ligament work was outside the body, and the trial did not establish fewer injuries or clinical tissue repair. Public and sports-institute support was disclosed.

sources.title: Aussieker et al.: Collagen, whey and early muscle connective-protein synthesis
sources.summary: Forty-five recreational athletes received collagen, whey or placebo after resistance exercise. Neither protein added a detectable increase in muscle connective-protein synthesis during the five-hour recovery observation.
sources.limitations: Acute, specified formulations and muscle tissue, not a long-term tendon or joint-treatment trial. Whey exceeded placebo for myofibrillar synthesis, but the whey-versus-collagen contrast was not significant. Relevant laboratory industry relationships, including collagen manufacturers, were disclosed.

sources.title: Clark et al.: Collagen hydrolysate and activity-related joint discomfort
sources.summary: A 24-week study of a specified collagen hydrolysate reported improvements in selected joint-discomfort measures among athletes.
sources.limitations: Of 147 recruited participants, 97 supplied statistically evaluable data; multiple outcomes and a post-hoc knee subgroup limit certainty. Findings concern symptoms, not cartilage regrowth, injury prevention or every collagen product. A branded commercial preparation was studied.

sources.title: Collagen hydrolysate and self-reported knee pain: Placebo-controlled trial
sources.summary: Compared collagen supplementation with placebo in people with self-reported knee pain and found no between-group improvement in the main pain measure.
sources.limitations: Specific preparation, selected population and outcome measures. A null trial does not disprove every collagen application; it illustrates why positive results elsewhere cannot be assumed universal. Consult the original for funding and disclosures.

sources.title: Lugo et al.: Undenatured type II collagen and knee osteoarthritis symptoms
sources.summary: Studied a specific chicken-cartilage-derived undenatured type II preparation over 180 days in adults with knee osteoarthritis. The preparation improved symptom scores relative to placebo in the trial.
sources.limitations: A specified product and selected osteoarthritis population, with commercial funding and manufacturer-affiliated authors. Symptom outcomes do not establish cartilage regrowth, the proposed immune mechanism or equivalence with hydrolysed collagen powders.

sources.title: Ohara et al.: Different collagen sources and circulating peptides
sources.summary: Compared fish-scale, fish-skin and porcine-skin type I gelatin hydrolysates in five healthy men; circulating peptide amounts and patterns differed.
sources.limitations: Five men, fasting conditions and biochemical outcomes. A higher peptide exposure for one preparation is not evidence of superior skin or joint outcomes. Authors had an industry laboratory affiliation.

sources.title: Proksch et al.: Specific peptides and skin physiology
sources.summary: A specific collagen hydrolysate improved measured skin elasticity versus placebo in a small eight-week study in women; not all measured skin outcomes improved significantly.
sources.limitations: Sixty-nine women aged 35–55, a specific ingredient and short follow-up. Results cannot certify all powders, predict every cosmetic outcome or settle the wider evidence-quality concerns.

sources.title: Lugo et al.: Undenatured type II collagen and knee symptoms
sources.summary: A 180-day study in adults with knee osteoarthritis compared a specific undenatured type II ingredient with placebo and glucosamine/chondroitin, reporting symptom-score improvements.
sources.limitations: Specific formulation and symptom outcomes, not proof of cartilage regeneration or a cure. Sponsor employees and a consultant coauthored the study. Gut immune tolerance is a proposed mechanism, not established by the clinical outcome alone.

sources.title: Aussieker et al.: Collagen, whey and post-exercise connective protein synthesis
sources.summary: In 45 young recreational athletes, whey increased myofibrillar synthesis versus placebo; neither whey nor collagen significantly increased muscle connective-protein synthesis over five hours.
sources.limitations: Acute tissue-specific measurements after one exercise session. Does not settle long-term tendon adaptation, every formulation or clinical rehabilitation.

sources.title: König et al.: Specific collagen peptides and postmenopausal bone density
sources.summary: A twelve-month study in postmenopausal women with reduced bone density reported changes in bone mineral density and bone-turnover markers with specific collagen peptides.
sources.limitations: Selected population and ingredient; bone-density findings do not establish fracture prevention or replacement of osteoporosis care. The study was partly supported by GELITA.

sources.title: Tripkovic et al.: D2 versus D3 food fortification in South Asian and white European women
sources.summary: A twelve-week UK food-fortification trial in 335 women found a greater increase in total 25-hydroxyvitamin D with D3 than with the tested D2 protocols.
sources.limitations: Status-marker outcome in specified populations and food vehicles; not proof of fracture prevention, universal clinical superiority, D2 inactivity or equivalence of all Indian retail products.

sources.title: Endocrine Society: Vitamin D for prevention of disease
sources.summary: Distinguishes routine prevention in generally healthy populations from established clinical indications, including recommendations concerning screening and supplementation schedules.
sources.limitations: Conditional recommendations with population-specific scope; does not replace an individualized plan for deficiency, relevant disease, pregnancy or other established indications. Not an India-specific prescribing guideline.

sources.title: Sanders et al.: Annual high-dose vitamin D and falls and fractures
sources.summary: The tested very large annual oral cholecalciferol regimen increased falls and fractures in older community-dwelling women.
sources.limitations: A specific high-dose annual schedule and selected older women; does not establish that every clinically supervised replacement regimen or ordinary vitamin D intake is harmful.

sources.title: MedlinePlus: Calcitriol medication information
sources.summary: Explains specified uses of calcitriol in calcium regulation and kidney or parathyroid disorders, together with monitoring and interaction considerations.
sources.limitations: Prescription medicine information, not a retail supplement recommendation or a conversion rule between activated medicines and ordinary nutritional D2 or D3.

sources.title: Schuster et al.: Magnesium bisglycinate in adults reporting poor sleep
sources.summary: A four-week placebo-controlled trial reported a modest between-group improvement in insomnia severity with the tested magnesium bisglycinate regimen.
sources.limitations: Short duration, self-reported outcomes and a small treatment effect; no head-to-head comparison with other magnesium salts, no universal insomnia-treatment claim and no verification of unrelated retail preparations.

sources.title: Roguin Maor et al.: Magnesium oxide for nocturnal leg cramps
sources.summary: In 94 predominantly older adults with recurrent nocturnal leg cramps, magnesium oxide was not superior to placebo during the four-week treatment phase.
sources.limitations: A particular preparation, population and duration; does not settle every cause of cramps, pregnancy-related cramps, exercise-associated symptoms or deficiency treatment.

sources.title: Wilborn et al.: ZMA and resistance-training adaptations
sources.summary: In 42 resistance-trained men, the tested ZMA preparation did not produce significant advantages over placebo in the reported hormone, body-composition or training outcomes over eight weeks.
sources.limitations: ZMA is a specific zinc-magnesium-aspartate preparation, not a trial of every ZMC combination; a null result in trained men does not negate correction of a diagnosed mineral deficiency.

sources.title: Purpura et al.: Liposomal vitamin C exposure in plasma and leukocytes
sources.summary: Compared single doses of a specified liposomal vitamin C preparation, ordinary vitamin C and placebo in 27 adults, reporting differences in measured vitamin C exposure.
sources.limitations: Acute pharmacokinetic outcomes for a particular commercial formulation; does not establish fewer infections, improved disease outcomes, superiority of every liposomal product or independent quality of an unrelated batch.

sources.title: Padayatty et al.: Oral versus intravenous vitamin C pharmacokinetics
sources.summary: Measured vitamin C concentrations and modelled exposure to show substantial differences between oral and intravenous administration routes.
sources.limitations: Pharmacokinetic investigation in healthy volunteers, not proof that an infusion improves routine wellness or that oral supplements inherit clinical claims from intravenous or laboratory experiments.

sources.title: NICE NG239: Vitamin B12 deficiency diagnosis and management
sources.summary: Makes assessment, oral or intramuscular replacement and follow-up decisions dependent on the cause and clinical context of vitamin B12 deficiency.
sources.limitations: UK clinical guidance for people aged over 16, not an individual Indian prescription or justification for self-diagnosis and replacement of prescribed treatment with a retail B-complex.

sources.title: Therapeutic Goods Administration: B6 and peripheral neuropathy
sources.summary: Describes nerve-related adverse events associated with supplemental B6 and the importance of overlapping products, including magnesium and zinc preparations that can also contain B6.
sources.limitations: Australian safety communication and adverse-event reports, not a prediction of individual risk or an assertion that Australian labelling law applies in India. Reports do not establish a universal harmless dose or duration.

sources.title: CDC: Common MTHFR variants and folic acid
sources.summary: Explains that people with common MTHFR variants can process folic acid and that common variants are not a reason to avoid the form with established neural tube defect prevention evidence.
sources.limitations: Discusses common variants and US public-health prevention advice; rare metabolic disorders and individual pregnancy or medicine-related plans require clinical assessment.

sources.title: NCCIH: Ashwagandha uses, interactions and safety limits
sources.summary: Summarises preparation variability, limited efficacy findings, short-term safety evidence, reported liver injury and condition- and medicine-related cautions.
sources.limitations: A US public-health overview, not certification of an Indian product, a diagnosis or an individual treatment plan.

sources.title: Bhatt et al.: Icosapent ethyl in the REDUCE-IT trial
sources.summary: In selected statin-treated high-risk patients with elevated triglycerides, the tested prescription EPA intervention reduced its primary cardiovascular endpoint compared with its comparator.
sources.limitations: A specific medicine, population, protocol and comparator; cannot establish equivalence or benefit for ordinary retail fish-oil mixtures. Read funding and safety results in the original.

sources.title: Nicholls et al.: EPA+DHA and cardiovascular outcomes in STRENGTH
sources.summary: A high-dose omega-3 carboxylic-acid formulation did not reduce the primary cardiovascular composite compared with corn oil in high-risk statin-treated participants; safety included an atrial-fibrillation signal.
sources.limitations: A particular formulation and clinical population, with a different comparator from REDUCE-IT. Results do not isolate a single cause of the difference between trials or validate untested retail products.

sources.title: Sinha et al.: Exploratory liposomal-glutathione study in adults
sources.summary: A small adult study reported changes in glutathione stores and selected immune-related markers after a specified liposomal preparation.
sources.limitations: Small exploratory design, biomarker outcomes and disclosed company involvement; not proof of better clinical outcomes or universal superiority to conventional oral glutathione.

sources.title: Erland and Saxena: Content variability in sampled melatonin products
sources.summary: Chemical analysis of selected Canadian melatonin products found discrepancies between measured and declared content and detected serotonin in some sampled products.
sources.limitations: Selected products and lots from one market. It does not establish the content, regulatory compliance or suitability of any untested Indian product or every delivery format.

sources.title: Cohen et al.: Measured melatonin and CBD in US gummies
sources.summary: An analytical study compared measured melatonin and CBD with declarations on sampled US gummy products and found frequent discrepancies.
sources.limitations: A selected US sample, not a test of Indian catalog products, every gummy formulation or a clinical comparison of sleep effects.

sources.title: Wall et al.: Long-term carnitine plus carbohydrate and muscle stores
sources.summary: A small prolonged protocol combining carnitine tartrate with carbohydrate increased muscle carnitine and altered selected exercise fuel-handling measures.
sources.limitations: Small study using substantial accompanying carbohydrate over 24 weeks; not a single-dose pre-workout experiment, a general fat-loss prescription or proof for every derivative.

sources.title: Villani et al.: Carnitine with aerobic training and body weight
sources.summary: The tested carnitine intervention with aerobic training did not promote additional weight loss in the studied moderately obese women.
sources.limitations: A selected female population and protocol; does not establish every clinical use or all derivative effects. It directly limits a universal mechanism-based fat-loss promise.

sources.title: Cholewa et al.: Betaine during training in collegiate women
sources.summary: An eight-week resistance-training study found selected body-fat differences but no added absolute-strength benefit with the tested betaine regimen.
sources.limitations: Untrained collegiate women, short follow-up and multiple outcomes; not proof for every athlete or a complete pre-workout formula. Includes an author with a commercial scientific-affairs affiliation.

sources.title: Moro et al.: Betaine during six weeks of CrossFit training
sources.summary: The specified betaine intervention did not add a measured hypertrophy or strength benefit over its comparator during six weeks of CrossFit training.
sources.limitations: A small and short sport-specific study, not a universal verdict across endurance tests, populations or formulations. Read intervention methods and commercial disclosures.

sources.title: Deutz et al.: Calcium HMB during short bed rest in older adults
sources.summary: A small ten-day bed-rest study suggested preservation of lean mass with calcium HMB under the tested protocol, without observed functional differences.
sources.limitations: Nineteen evaluable participants, sensitivity to an excluded participant and limited functional power; requires confirmation and cannot establish a general muscle-wasting treatment. Read commercial affiliations and funding.

sources.title: HMB versus leucine alongside whey during resistance training
sources.summary: Compared whey plus calcium HMB with whey plus leucine during a resistance-training programme and found no difference in measured muscle-size or strength gains.
sources.limitations: Specific young male participants, protein background and comparator; not a formal statement that every form or clinical context is equivalent.

sources.title: Campbell et al.: AAKG pharmacokinetics and training outcomes in adult men
sources.summary: Examined AAKG exposure and, in a separate eight-week resistance-training experiment, found advantages for selected strength and power outcomes without differences in several other measured endpoints.
sources.limitations: Specific AAKG preparation and protocols in adult men. It does not establish universal superiority to free arginine, validate every retail formulation or supply an individual dosing recommendation. Read the study's funding and commercial context.

sources.title: Wax et al.: Acute AAKG and resistance-exercise performance
sources.summary: An acute placebo-controlled crossover experiment in trained and untrained men found no improvement in its tested maximal-strength or total-load-volume measures with AAKG.
sources.limitations: Sixteen participants, one acute protocol and particular exercises. A null result does not establish equivalence or settle every preparation, exposure period or population.

sources.title: Howatson et al.: BCAA after deliberately damaging exercise
sources.summary: A small placebo-controlled study in resistance-trained men found favourable differences in soreness, creatine-kinase response and recovery of maximal voluntary contraction after a damaging drop-jump protocol; other measurements did not differ.
sources.limitations: Twelve men and a deliberately damaging exercise bout. These recovery measures are not evidence of greater long-term muscle gain, a universal need for BCAAs or superiority of every marketed ratio.

sources.title: Waldron et al.: BCAA and recovery from a hypertrophy exercise bout
sources.summary: Measured soreness, muscle function and creatine kinase after a diet-controlled hypertrophy exercise session, reporting favourable selected recovery comparisons with the tested BCAA protocol.
sources.limitations: Sixteen resistance-trained participants with a specified mixture and acute exercise protocol. Small-sample, endpoint-specific findings do not demonstrate indefinite benefit, an optimal ratio or improved long-term adaptation.

sources.title: Dillon et al.: Essential amino acids, lean mass and strength in older women
sources.summary: In a small three-month study of older women, EAA supplementation was associated with increased lean body mass and basal muscle protein synthesis, while the tested strength measure remained unchanged.
sources.limitations: Fourteen women in a selected older-adult population. Changes in composition and synthesis do not establish improved function, a sarcopenia cure or an identical response to every retail EAA product or in younger athletes.

sources.title: Lutsch et al.: A multi-ingredient pre-workout and five-kilometre running
