sources.summary: A particular caffeine-containing pre-workout did not improve the measured five-kilometre running-time or subjective-fatigue outcomes compared with placebo in aerobically trained adults.
sources.limitations: Twenty participants, one finished mixture and an acute running task. The result neither validates nor rejects every blend and cannot isolate the contribution of each ingredient without relevant component comparisons.

sources.title: Dose and timing of caffeine and subsequent sleep: Randomized crossover trial
sources.summary: Compared two caffeine amounts at several pre-bed intervals in men. The larger amount disrupted subsequent sleep under conditions where the lower amount showed a different pattern.
sources.limitations: Twenty-three men with specified habitual intake and exposures. It does not establish a universal safe bedtime cutoff, identical effects in women or a personalized caffeine limit. Published online in 2024 and in its journal issue in 2025.

sources.title: Hill et al.: Beta-alanine, muscle carnosine and cycling capacity
sources.summary: Repeated beta-alanine supplementation increased measured muscle carnosine and was accompanied by changes in a specified high-intensity cycling-capacity test.
sources.limitations: Small study in men, specific ingredient and laboratory task, with fewer participants completing longer follow-up. It does not establish improvement in every sport or validate an occasional pre-workout serving. Journal issue 2007; online publication 2006.

sources.title: Derave et al.: Carnosine, repeated contractions and race performance in sprinters
sources.summary: In trained male sprinters, beta-alanine increased muscle carnosine and attenuated fatigue in selected repeated-contraction bouts, without improving the tested isometric-endurance or indoor race-time outcomes.
sources.limitations: Fifteen male athletes, four-week exposure and specific tests. A laboratory fatigue finding cannot be generalized to every competition or to long-term muscle growth.

sources.title: Decombaz et al.: Slow-release beta-alanine absorption and sensory symptoms
sources.summary: Compared a beta-alanine solution with a specific slow-release tablet and placebo, finding changes in absorption kinetics and reported sensory symptoms with the tested delivery system.
sources.limitations: Eleven healthy adults and acute absorption/tolerability outcomes, not a performance or hypertrophy trial. It does not certify all sustained-release products. A published erratum and the commercial research affiliations should be read alongside the paper.

sources.title: Balshaw et al.: Isolated taurine and a three-kilometre running trial
sources.summary: A small placebo-controlled crossover experiment reported improved performance in a specified running-time trial after acute isolated taurine in trained middle-distance runners.
sources.limitations: Small trained-runner sample, acute exposure and one task. It does not establish alertness, every exercise outcome or effectiveness of a multi-ingredient energy drink. Journal publication 2013; published online 2012.

sources.title: Energy-drink ingredients: Independent and combined caffeine and taurine effects
sources.summary: Separated caffeine and taurine contributions to a behavioural reaction-time task, finding an effect associated with caffeine without establishing an independent taurine advantage in that test.
sources.limitations: Small sample of young women, particular amounts and a behavioural endpoint. It does not settle every taurine application, quantify exercise benefit or validate every finished energy drink.

sources.title: Caffeine plus taurine and cycling in the heat: Crossover trial
sources.summary: In a small exercise-in-heat experiment, combined caffeine and taurine did not improve time to exhaustion compared with placebo despite changes in ventilatory and metabolic demand.
sources.limitations: Ten non-heat-acclimated adults and a specific co-ingestion protocol. It does not establish that all combinations are ineffective or identify the isolated contribution of each ingredient.

sources.title: Peel et al.: Taurine, sweating and heat balance under controlled humidity
sources.summary: Studied low-intensity exercise at fixed heat production in hot conditions with controlled humidity, reporting increased sweating and evaporative cooling after the tested taurine exposure.
sources.limitations: Fifteen selected adults, a controlled workload and environment, and thermoregulation outcomes. It does not replace fluid or electrolyte planning, establish prevention of heat illness or provide a universal hot-weather prescription.

sources.title: Simmonds et al.: Taurine during exercise after cold exposure with forced airflow
sources.summary: In men exercising after moderate cold exposure with forced airflow, taurine did not significantly improve the tested endurance outcome or several temperature and local-sweating measurements.
sources.limitations: Eleven men and a specific cold-air protocol. It is not a direct replication of a hot-humidity trial; environmental conditions and the chosen outcome need to remain explicit. Journal issue 2022; online publication 2020.

sources.title: Dawson-Hughes et al.: Meal conditions affect vitamin D3 absorption but not the later 25-hydroxyvitamin D response
sources.summary: Meal conditions affected early absorption, but the later blood-status response did not differ significantly between groups.
sources.limitations: 62 older healthy adults and a specific repeated-dose protocol; no clinical outcome endpoint.

sources.title: Raimundo et al.: Fat-containing meals and 25-hydroxyvitamin D after a single vitamin D dose
sources.summary: A single-dose experiment found a larger subsequent blood-status rise when the meal contained more fat.
sources.limitations: Young healthy adults with low mean baseline status; one dose and short follow-up, without clinical outcomes. Online publication 2014; journal issue 2015.

sources.title: Terink et al.: Blood magnesium falls after exercise and restores within hours
sources.summary: Ionised and total magnesium concentrations temporarily declined after an endurance exercise bout and returned to baseline within hours on average.
sources.limitations: 18 trained endurance athletes; monitoring study rather than a supplementation efficacy trial. Online publication 2016; issue 2017.

sources.title: Veronese et al.: Magnesium and physical function in older women undertaking an exercise programme
sources.summary: Selected everyday-function measures improved, with a stronger signal among women with lower dietary intake; secondary strength differences were not significant.
sources.limitations: Older women, twelve weeks and a no-intervention comparator rather than placebo; not evidence of athletic enhancement.

sources.title: Wood and Zheng: High dietary calcium intake, zinc absorption and balance
sources.kind: Controlled human feeding and acute absorption experiments
sources.summary: Added calcium reduced zinc absorption and balance in the tested feeding protocol; a separate acute meal experiment also found inhibition.
sources.limitations: Selected participants, meals and supplemental exposures; does not establish zinc deficiency from ordinary dairy intake.

sources.title: Hunt and Beiseigel: Dietary calcium did not worsen phytate inhibition of zinc absorption from conventional diets
sources.summary: Phytate reduced zinc absorption, while higher calcium did not significantly impair it in the tested ordinary-food menus.
sources.limitations: Ten healthy women and one-day menus; not a long-term trial of every concentrated mineral combination.

sources.title: Mock et al.: Markers during experimentally induced biotin deficiency and repletion
sources.summary: Urinary biotin and a metabolic by-product changed during experimental depletion and recovered during repletion.
sources.limitations: Eleven healthy adults on an artificial depletion diet; no hair-growth outcome and no consumer self-testing protocol.

sources.title: Eng et al.: Identification and assessment of markers of biotin status in healthy adults
sources.kind: Controlled human feeding and biomarker study
sources.summary: Twenty candidate markers differed in their ability to distinguish deficient, sufficient and supplemented states.
sources.limitations: Sixteen healthy adults; research-marker assessment rather than validation of a cosmetic claim or a retail diagnostic threshold.

sources.title: NHS: Hair loss, possible causes and assessment
sources.summary: Describes several causes of hair loss and when assessment is appropriate.
sources.limitations: General guidance; cannot diagnose an individual cause or establish a nutrient treatment indication. Page reviewed in 2024.

sources.title: Paulsen et al.: Vitamin C and E, cellular adaptation and endurance training
sources.summary: Selected mitochondrial protein responses were blunted without a significant difference in the measured aerobic-capacity and running improvements.
sources.limitations: Combined C and E in 54 young adults over eleven weeks; cannot isolate vitamin C or establish every long-term performance effect.

sources.title: Paulsen et al.: Vitamin C and E, strength-training signalling and muscle growth
sources.summary: Some signalling and strength responses were smaller, but muscle growth and acute protein-synthesis differences were not significant.
sources.limitations: 32 recreationally trained adults over ten weeks; a combined regimen with tentative strength findings.

sources.title: Ristow et al.: Antioxidants and metabolic responses to physical training in humans
sources.summary: Combined C and E attenuated some training-associated insulin-sensitivity and endogenous antioxidant responses.
sources.limitations: Small four-week study in healthy men, including open-label and blinded parts; no incident-diabetes outcome and no isolation of vitamin C.

sources.title: de Jager et al.: Long-term metformin and risk of B12 deficiency
sources.summary: Long-term metformin reduced B12 concentrations and increased biochemical deficiency risk compared with placebo.
sources.limitations: Insulin-treated adults with type 2 diabetes; does not individualise symptom causation, monitoring or replacement.

sources.title: Aroda et al.: B12 deficiency during the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study
sources.kind: Secondary analysis of a trial and extended follow-up
sources.summary: Longer metformin exposure was associated with biochemical B12 deficiency during extended follow-up.
sources.limitations: Follow-up included open-label treatment; later neurological associations are not equivalent to randomised proof of their cause.

sources.title: MHRA: Metformin, reduced vitamin B12 and monitoring people at risk
sources.summary: Advises assessment when deficiency is suspected, risk-based monitoring and continuing appropriate metformin while B12 is corrected.
sources.limitations: UK professional safety advice, not a universal self-testing schedule or an Indian regulatory claim.

sources.title: Lonn et al.: HOPE-2 homocysteine lowering with folic acid and B vitamins
sources.summary: The combination lowered homocysteine without significantly improving the primary cardiovascular composite; stroke was lower individually.
sources.limitations: High-risk adults and combined folate/B6/B12; secondary stroke finding should not replace the primary result.

sources.title: Huo et al.: CSPPT folic acid added to hypertension treatment for first-stroke prevention
sources.summary: Adding folic acid to enalapril reduced first strokes compared with enalapril alone in the studied population.
sources.limitations: Chinese adults with hypertension, no previous stroke or myocardial infarction and no folic-acid fortification background; not universal prevention advice.

sources.title: Albert et al.: VITAL Rhythm marine omega-3 and incident atrial fibrillation
sources.summary: Marine EPA plus DHA did not significantly change incident AF compared with placebo in the primary-prevention population.
sources.limitations: Studied regimen and older adults without prior AF or cardiovascular disease; not proof of zero risk or equivalence to higher-dose treatment.

sources.title: American Heart Association: Fish within a healthy dietary pattern
sources.summary: Recommends fish within a healthy dietary pattern and describes the association between regular seafood consumption and cardiovascular health.
sources.limitations: Food-pattern advice does not validate every retail supplement or establish a prescription indication. Page reviewed in 2024.

sources.title: NHLBI: Atrial fibrillation symptoms and assessment
sources.summary: Explains that AF may be asymptomatic or cause symptoms such as palpitations, fatigue and breathlessness.
sources.limitations: Symptoms are not a self-diagnosis; this page does not attribute AF to an individual supplement. Updated 2022.

sources.title: Mamerow et al. (2014): Dietary protein distribution positively influences 24-h muscle protein synthesis in healthy adults
sources.summary: Eight adults consumed equal-protein diets distributed evenly or toward dinner. The even pattern increased measured daily muscle protein synthesis during short feeding periods.
sources.limitations: Very small, short experiment with a tracer endpoint; no long-term strength or hypertrophy outcome. Authors disclosed relevant speaking compensation.

sources.title: Kim et al. (2018): Protein intake distribution pattern does not affect anabolic response, lean body mass, muscle strength or function over 8 weeks in older adults
sources.summary: Fourteen older adults received even or dinner-heavy protein distributions with similar daily intake. Measured body-composition, function and anabolic outcomes did not differ significantly.
sources.limitations: Only seven participants per group and eight weeks of follow-up. Healthy older volunteers do not represent all frail or clinical populations. Published online in 2017, journal issue in 2018.

sources.title: Justesen et al. (2022): Comparing even with skewed dietary protein distribution shows no difference in muscle protein synthesis or amino acid utilization in healthy older individuals
sources.summary: Integrated tracer measurements found similar muscle protein synthesis and dietary amino-acid utilisation with even and skewed protein distributions when total intake was sufficient.
sources.limitations: Controlled short-term feeding in healthy older adults; not a long-term trial of disability, frailty or an individually optimal meal schedule.

sources.title: Gordji-Nejad et al. (2024): Single dose creatine improves cognitive performance and induces changes in cerebral high energy phosphates during sleep deprivation
sources.summary: A fifteen-person crossover experiment during sleep deprivation reported selected cognitive improvements and changes in brain high-energy phosphates after a single experimental creatine exposure.
sources.limitations: Small acute laboratory experiment using a high body-mass-based exposure. Does not establish routine dosing, safe driving, replacement of sleep or treatment of neurological disease.

sources.title: EFSA NDA Panel (2024): Creatine and improvement in cognitive function—evaluation of a proposed health claim
sources.summary: The panel assessed submitted human intervention evidence and concluded that a cause-and-effect relationship between creatine supplementation and improved cognitive function had not been established.
sources.limitations: A dated assessment of a defined proposed claim. It is not a trial, a statement of Indian law or a ruling on every possible future clinical use.

sources.title: Jerger et al. (2022): Effects of specific collagen peptide supplementation combined with resistance training on Achilles tendon properties
sources.summary: Specific collagen peptides plus fourteen weeks of resistance training produced a greater Achilles tendon area adaptation than the same training with placebo in healthy male volunteers.
sources.limitations: Structural and performance endpoints in healthy participants do not prove injury prevention or healing. Gelita paid part of the costs and one author disclosed collagen-related patents.

sources.title: Miyamoto et al. (2025): Collagen peptide supplementation enhances muscle-tendon stiffness and explosive strength—a 16-wk randomized controlled trial
sources.summary: Fifty young sedentary men received collagen peptides or placebo for sixteen weeks. The investigators reported changes in stiffness and selected rapid-torque measures without increased area or maximal voluntary torque.
sources.limitations: Not an injured-tendon or resistance-training rehabilitation trial. Abstract within-group significance should not be treated as proof of every between-group contrast. Includes an industry research affiliation.

sources.title: Praet et al. (2019): Oral supplementation of specific collagen peptides combined with calf-strengthening exercises enhances function and reduces pain in Achilles tendinopathy patients
sources.summary: Twenty patients with chronic mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy followed a calf-strengthening and return-to-running programme. Symptom-and-function scores improved more during the specific collagen-peptide periods.
sources.limitations: Small commercially funded pilot, proprietary preparation and potential carryover. No supplement-only arm, acute-rupture evidence or demonstration of complete repair. Sponsor funded the study; authors stated no sponsor role in analysis or publication.

sources.title: Björnsson et al. (2020): Ashwagandha-induced liver injury—a case series from Iceland and the US Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network
sources.summary: Five investigated cases developed jaundice with cholestatic or mixed liver injury after ashwagandha-containing products. Available product analysis supported exposure, with alternative causes considered.
sources.limitations: No exposed-user denominator or randomized comparator. Several patients used additional supplements; a case series cannot estimate incidence or identify an exact individual risk.

sources.title: Philips et al. (2023): Ashwagandha-induced liver injury—a case series from India and literature review
sources.summary: The report describes eight selected single-ingredient exposure cases from three Indian hospitals. Several patients had chronic liver disease, and severe outcomes occurred in that subgroup.
sources.limitations: Retrospective referral-selected cases with causality uncertainty and no exposed-user denominator. Cannot establish prevalence, incidence or a brand-wide risk estimate.

sources.title: NIH LiverTox (updated 2024): Ashwagandha
sources.summary: Describes reported clinically apparent liver injury, its usual clinical pattern, uncertainty about the responsible components, and particular concern in advanced chronic liver disease.
sources.limitations: A clinical synthesis based largely on reports and series, not an incidence study. Likelihood-of-causation assessment is not a percentage risk for users.

sources.title: Kumar et al. (2023): Supplementing glycine and N-acetylcysteine in older adults improves glutathione deficiency and selected metabolic and physical-function measures
sources.summary: Twenty-four older adults were randomized to sixteen weeks of GlyNAC or alanine placebo. The study reported favourable changes across several biochemical and functional outcomes.
sources.limitations: Twelve per randomized arm, many endpoints and exploratory analyses. Does not isolate individual ingredients or demonstrate human life extension or disease prevention. Online in 2022; 2023 journal issue.

sources.title: Lizzo et al. (2022): A randomized controlled clinical trial in healthy older adults to determine efficacy of glycine and N-acetylcysteine supplementation on glutathione redox status and oxidative damage
sources.summary: In 114 older completers, two weeks of GlyNAC did not significantly improve the primary total-glutathione endpoint. A post-hoc subgroup suggested a possible response in participants with greater oxidative stress and lower baseline glutathione.
sources.limitations: Short exposure; subgroup findings require confirmation. Authors disclosed Nestlé employment and product-related patents and licences. Different population and duration from the smaller sixteen-week trial.

sources.title: Wright et al. (2026): Management of shift work disorder—an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline
sources.summary: Separates excessive sleepiness, sleep disturbance and circadian adaptation. Melatonin suggestions for selected sleep settings are conditional, with low or very-low-certainty evidence and attention to residual sleepiness.
sources.limitations: Individual clinical judgement remains necessary; many underlying studies used simulated shifts or workers without a formal disorder diagnosis. Does not establish long-term disease prevention or universal dosing. Final publication 24 October 2026.

sources.title: Wright et al. (2026): Management of shift work disorder—an AASM systematic review, meta-analysis and GRADE assessment
sources.summary: Evaluates interventions by sleepiness, sleep disturbance and circadian goals, with study-population and clinical-importance assessments. Highlights uncertainty and the need for longer-term health-outcome studies.
sources.limitations: Certainty is limited for many interventions, including melatonin questions. This companion review and guideline are not independent experiments. Published 24 October 2026.

sources.title: Yoon et al. (2002): Role of morning melatonin administration and attenuation of sunlight exposure in improving adaptation of night-shift workers
sources.summary: A twelve-nurse experiment found modest sleep-time improvement with morning melatonin but no clear benefit on performance tests; alertness findings were limited.
sources.limitations: Very small sample and short conditions; cannot establish individual driving safety, durable adaptation or effects of every work schedule.

sources.title: Jorgensen and Witting (1998): Randomized clinical trial of melatonin after night-shift work—efficacy and neuropsychologic effects
sources.summary: Fifteen emergency physicians completed placebo and melatonin periods after consecutive night shifts. The study did not show a clear recovery benefit in its sleep, tiredness or neuropsychological outcomes.
sources.limitations: Small occupational sample with a specific schedule; a null result does not exclude benefit in different sleep contexts.

sources.title: Sadeghniiat-Haghighi et al. (2016): Melatonin therapy in shift workers with difficulty falling asleep—a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled crossover field study
sources.kind: Primary human randomized crossover field trial
sources.summary: Thirty-nine workers completed the short study periods. Sleep-onset latency and efficiency improved, without a clear total-sleep-time or wake-after-sleep-onset benefit.
sources.limitations: Selected workers with sleep-onset difficulty and short exposure. The assessed sleep was nighttime sleep, so results should not be relabelled as all daytime post-shift sleep or on-duty alertness.

sources.title: Koeth et al. (2013): Intestinal microbiota metabolism of L-carnitine, a nutrient in red meat, promotes atherosclerosis
sources.kind: Primary human mechanistic and observational research with animal experiments
sources.summary: Human challenges demonstrated microbiota-dependent TMAO formation and diet-related response differences. A separate cardiac cohort and mouse experiments supplied observational and mechanistic cardiovascular evidence.
sources.limitations: Not a randomized human trial of supplement-induced cardiovascular events. Animal mechanisms and associations in referred patients cannot quantify a healthy user's clinical risk.

sources.title: Koeth et al. (2019): L-carnitine in omnivorous diets induces an atherogenic gut microbial pathway in humans
sources.kind: Primary human isotope-tracer and microbiome study
sources.summary: Tracers and microbial experiments characterised sequential carnitine-to-TMA transformations and how repeated exposure can induce pathway activity.
sources.limitations: Mechanistic metabolite outcomes do not establish clinical-event risk or guarantee any individual's response based on dietary identity. Online in 2018; journal issue in 2019.

sources.title: Samulak et al. (2019): L-carnitine supplementation increases trimethylamine-N-oxide but not markers of atherosclerosis in healthy aged women
sources.summary: During twenty-four weeks of supplementation, TMAO rose substantially without deterioration in the selected lipid, inflammatory and vascular markers measured.
sources.limitations: Small selected population and biomarker outcomes; no adequate assessment of heart attacks, strokes or long-term safety. Online in 2018; journal issue in 2019.

sources.title: Samulak et al. (2019): Plasma trimethylamine-N-oxide following cessation of L-carnitine supplementation in healthy aged women
sources.summary: TMAO returned to a level comparable with placebo four months after stopping supplementation and remained stable at a later follow-up; measured lipid profiles did not materially change.
sources.limitations: Same underlying small older-women cohort, not independent replication. Reversibility of a marker does not establish lifetime cardiovascular safety.

sources.title: Olthof et al. (2003): Low dose betaine supplementation leads to immediate and long-term lowering of plasma homocysteine in healthy men and women
sources.summary: Controlled betaine exposure lowered fasting and methionine-load homocysteine responses, including a dose-related fasting effect over six weeks.
sources.limitations: Biochemical outcomes rather than clinical cardiovascular events. Experimental regimens do not constitute a personal prescription.

sources.title: Olthof et al. (2005): Effect of homocysteine-lowering nutrients on blood lipids—results from four randomised placebo-controlled studies in healthy humans
sources.kind: Primary analysis of randomized human trials
sources.summary: The analysis included three betaine studies with 151 participants. The higher tested regimen increased LDL cholesterol and triglycerides relative to placebo during short controlled exposure.
sources.limitations: No clinical-event outcome; effects should not be generalized to every amount, duration or population. Data overlap contributing homocysteine studies and are not wholly independent replication.

sources.title: Zawieja et al. (2022): The effect of 3-week betaine supplementation on blood biomarkers of cardiometabolic health in young physically active males
sources.summary: A three-week double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study reported lower homocysteine without clear effects on lipids, selected cytokines or liver enzymes.
sources.limitations: Short study in selected healthy active men with biomarker endpoints; cannot establish clinical cardiovascular benefit or long-term safety.

sources.title: HOPE-2 Investigators (2006): Homocysteine lowering with folic acid and B vitamins in vascular disease
sources.summary: In 5,522 high-risk participants followed for about five years, a B-vitamin intervention lowered homocysteine without reducing the primary composite of major cardiovascular events.
sources.limitations: Tested B vitamins, not betaine. Illustrates why surrogate changes need clinical-outcome testing; it does not directly establish betaine's efficacy or lack of efficacy. Individual outcomes differed.

sources.title: Wilson et al.: Oral arginine in peripheral arterial disease (NO-PAIN)
sources.summary: Six months of oral arginine in 133 patients with intermittent claudication increased plasma arginine without the intended vascular or walking benefit; walking improvement was smaller than with placebo.
sources.limitations: Patients with peripheral arterial disease, not healthy athletes. Does not estimate risk or efficacy in other populations.

sources.title: Bode-Böger et al.: Intravenous arginine and blood flow in critical limb ischemia
sources.summary: Acute intravenous arginine increased blood flow in patients with critical limb ischemia.
sources.limitations: Intravenous administration and an acute physiological endpoint; cannot validate oral retail supplements or training outcomes.

sources.title: Longland et al.: Higher protein during energy restriction and intensive exercise
sources.summary: Forty young men completed a four-week energy-restriction and intensive-exercise protocol. Higher dietary protein produced greater lean-mass gain and fat-mass loss than lower protein.
sources.limitations: A short, demanding controlled protocol; not a BCAA trial or a universal dieting prescription.

sources.title: Mettler et al.: Dietary protein and lean-mass retention during athlete weight loss
sources.summary: Twenty trained young athletes underwent two weeks of energy restriction. Higher protein reduced lean-body-mass loss; performance and fat loss did not differ.
sources.limitations: Short duration and selected healthy trained population; lean mass is not identical to contractile muscle. Does not test isolated BCAA.

sources.title: Kim et al.: Exercise and leucine-rich amino acids in older women with sarcopenia
sources.summary: Compared exercise, leucine-rich amino acids, their combination and health education over three months in 155 Japanese women aged at least 75. Outcomes included leg mass, walking speed and knee-extension strength.
sources.limitations: Specific selected female population and programme; within-group improvement alone cannot establish between-group superiority. The record includes a published erratum.

sources.title: Børsheim et al.: Amino acids, muscle and physical function in older adults
sources.summary: Twelve older adults received an essential-amino-acid plus arginine mixture for 16 weeks; muscle-related and physical-function measures improved.
sources.limitations: No concurrent control; cannot isolate the supplement from practice effects, behavioural changes or other influences, or isolate EAA from arginine.

sources.title: Geyer et al.: Undeclared anabolic steroids in non-hormonal supplements
sources.summary: Tested 634 supplements bought in 13 countries during 2000–2001; 94 contained undeclared anabolic-androgenic steroids.
sources.limitations: Historical selected sample, not current Indian prevalence. Analytical matrix effects prevented reliable results for 66 products.

sources.title: Cohen et al.: Higenamine in weight-loss and sports supplements
sources.summary: Twenty-four products listing higenamine or related names showed widely varying measured amounts; the five declaring a quantity did not state it accurately.
sources.limitations: Targeted US product selection, not market prevalence or a current batch verdict. Some authors disclosed certification-industry employment. Published online 2018; journal issue 2019.

sources.title: UK Anti-Doping: Managing supplement risks
sources.summary: Explains athlete responsibility, supplement risk assessment and the limits of batch testing; WADA and UKAD do not approve supplements.
sources.limitations: UK authority explaining the anti-doping framework; not Indian retail product approval or an assurance of zero risk. Athletes must follow their own applicable authority and current rules.

sources.title: USADA: Supplement Connect
sources.summary: Resources for evaluating supplements and third-party certification, including why screening can reduce but cannot eliminate risk.
sources.limitations: Programmes and their scope differ; guidance is not a guarantee of efficacy, safety or absence of every prohibited substance.

sources.title: USADA: TrueSport Nutrition Guide 2026, supplement certification guidance
sources.summary: Explains that supplement certification programmes differ in their testing coverage and frequency, and reduce rather than eliminate contamination risk.
sources.limitations: Not every programme tests every batch or every prohibited substance; certification is not a performance endorsement or a guarantee.

sources.title: Suzuki et al.: L-citrulline and a four-kilometre cycling time trial
sources.summary: Repeated oral L-citrulline improved four-kilometre cycling time-trial performance in 22 trained men under the tested protocol.
sources.limitations: Small male sample and specific short event; manufacturer-affiliated authors. Not proof for other endurance events or lifting.

sources.title: Cunniffe et al.: Acute citrulline malate and high-intensity cycling
sources.summary: In ten well-trained men, plasma citrulline increased after acute citrulline malate without improved repeated-sprint or subsequent exhaustion outcomes.
sources.limitations: Small sample and acute malate protocol, not a direct replication of repeated free-citrulline time-trial studies.

sources.title: Ducker et al.: Beta-alanine and 800-metre running performance
sources.summary: Eighteen male recreational club runners completed duplicate pre/post track tests around 28 days of supplementation; adjusted 800-metre race times favoured beta-alanine.
sources.limitations: Nine participants per group; a specific male recreational running population. Group results are not guaranteed individual time gains.

sources.title: Chung et al.: Carnosine loading without one-hour cycling improvement
sources.summary: Six weeks in 27 trained cyclists and triathletes substantially increased muscle carnosine without improving laboratory one-hour time-trial performance relative to placebo.
sources.limitations: A particular longer event protocol; not a verdict on all shorter or intermittent exercise.

sources.title: Li et al.: Taurine and vascular function in type 2 diabetes
sources.summary: A twelve-week trial randomized 165 adults with type 2 diabetes, with 144 completing the protocol with complete data. Reported improvements included systolic pressure and vascular-function measures.
sources.limitations: Short duration, attrition and surrogate outcomes; no demonstration of reduced cardiovascular events, diabetic complications or healthy-athlete benefit.

sources.title: Moludi et al.: Taurine added to a low-calorie diet in type 2 diabetes
sources.summary: An eight-week trial in 120 patients found improvements in insulin-resistance estimates and selected inflammatory/endothelial markers, but not fasting glucose, glycated haemoglobin or lipids. Both arms followed a low-calorie diet.
sources.limitations: Short adjunctive study, multiple biomarkers and no complication endpoint. The September 2022 correction fixes an affiliation rather than the reported outcomes.

sources.title: Deutz et al.: Specialised oral nutrition in malnourished hospital patients (NOURISH)
sources.summary: In 652 enrolled older malnourished hospital patients, high-protein HMB-containing oral nutrition did not significantly improve the primary 90-day death/readmission composite. Secondary mortality was lower; readmission was not different.
sources.limitations: Nutrition package differed in energy, protein and other components, preventing HMB-only attribution. Selected diagnoses, attrition and Abbott funding/manufacturer involvement limit interpretation.
